name: Rolle's Theorem & Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem
whatIsIt: ROLLE'S THEOREM: if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b) (same height at both ends), then SOMEWHERE in between the tangent must be perfectly flat — there exists c in (a, b) with f′(c) = 0. LAGRANGE'S MEAN VALUE THEOREM (MVT) is the general version without the equal-heights rule: it guarantees a point c where the INSTANTANEOUS slope f′(c) exactly equals the AVERAGE slope over the whole interval, f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
whyNeeded: These two theorems are the bridge between a curve's overall behaviour (its endpoints) and its local slope at one specific point — the mathematical backbone of almost every 'somewhere in between' argument in calculus, and a standard proof-based JEE Advanced topic. MVT is also literally how speeding tickets work: if your average speed over a stretch was 100 km/h, MVT guarantees your speedometer showed EXACTLY 100 km/h at some instant.
realLifeUses: Speed cameras: if your average speed between two points was above the limit, MVT proves your instantaneous speed matched it at some moment
Proving a rocket's velocity must have equalled its average velocity at some instant during flight
Engineering: guaranteeing a beam's stress rate matches its average stress rate somewhere along its length
The theoretical foundation behind why derivatives can locate roots and turning points reliably

story.title: The Speed Camera
story.text: Kabir drives from the toll gate to the exit, 100 km, in exactly 1 hour — an average speed of 100 km/h. 'But I never once looked at 100 on my speedometer!' he protests. The officer smiles: 'Doesn't matter what you SAW. Your position is a continuous, differentiable function of time. By Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem, at SOME instant during that hour, your instantaneous speed must have equalled your average speed — exactly 100 km/h.' Kabir has no comeback; the theorem guarantees it, whether he noticed or not.
story.extractedProblem: If a car's average speed over a 1-hour trip was 100 km/h, what does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee?
story.answerInStory: That at some exact instant during the trip, the car's instantaneous speed was exactly 100 km/h.

standardMethod.summary: For Rolle's Theorem: check f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), verify f(a) = f(b), then solve f′(c) = 0 for c in (a,b). For Lagrange's MVT: check continuity/differentiability, compute the average slope (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), then solve f′(c) equal to that average slope for c in (a,b).
steps: Confirm f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) — both theorems require this.
For Rolle's: check f(a) = f(b). If true, solve f′(c) = 0 for c strictly between a and b.
For Lagrange's MVT: compute the average slope (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).
Solve f′(c) = average slope for c, and confirm c lies strictly between a and b.
Rolle's Theorem is just Lagrange's MVT in the special case where the average slope happens to be 0.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying Rolle's Theorem without first checking f(a) = f(b).
commonMistakes.fix: Rolle's Theorem ONLY applies when f(a) = f(b). If the endpoints have different heights, you need Lagrange's MVT instead, not Rolle's.

commonMistakes.mistake: Computing the average slope as f(b) − f(a) alone, forgetting to divide by (b − a).
commonMistakes.fix: The average (mean) slope is (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a) — always divide by the width of the interval, not just the change in height.

teachBackPrompt: Draw a bumpy curve from (1, 0) up and back down to (3, 0). Show a grown-up why Rolle's Theorem guarantees a flat tangent somewhere in between, then explain how Lagrange's MVT is the same idea but for a chord that isn't flat — the tangent matches the chord's slope somewhere, not necessarily zero.

revisionCard.summary: Rolle's Theorem: f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), f(a)=f(b) ⇒ f′(c)=0 for some c in (a,b). Lagrange's MVT (the general version): f′(c) = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a) for some c in (a,b) — instantaneous slope equals average slope somewhere. Rolle's is MVT when the average slope is 0.

rememberIt.hook: Rolle's: equal ends → flat tangent somewhere. Lagrange's: tangent matches the average slope somewhere
rememberIt.unpack: Both need continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Rolle's is Lagrange's MVT with average slope = 0.

studentQuestions.q: Why does Rolle's Theorem need differentiability, not just continuity?
studentQuestions.a: Continuity alone guarantees the curve has no breaks, but a sharp corner (like |x|) can be continuous yet have no well-defined tangent slope there — differentiability guarantees a genuine tangent exists at every interior point to search among.

No — speed is just the easiest example. MVT applies to ANY continuous, differentiable function: temperature change, population growth rate, cost curves, anything with an average rate of change over an interval.
